title: 008 — Databricks multi-statement transactions are generally available
html:
008 — Databricks multi-statement transactions are generally available

The one idea: Databricks now commits several SQL statements across several tables as one atomic unit. They all succeed or none do. That was the last big warehouse feature lakehouses lacked. Patterns like "update orders and inventory together" and write-audit-publish no longer need custom retry and reconciliation code.

Added 2026-10-17 · Announced 2026-10-16 by Databricks

1. What it is

Multi-statement, multi-table transactions are generally available on Unity Catalog managed Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables. There are two styles:

Style How it ends Runs on Concurrency
Non-interactive: BEGIN ATOMIC … END Commits on success and rolls back on any error Any SQL warehouse, serverless compute, or a cluster on Databricks Runtime 18.0+ Row-level, if the target tables have row-level concurrency enabled
Interactive: BEGIN TRANSACTION You run COMMIT or ROLLBACK SQL warehouses Table-level

Transactions work with temporary tables, stored procedures, SQL scripting and streaming tables. Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply inside them.

2. Why it matters

  • No more half-finished loads. Without transactions, a job that updates a fact table and then a summary table can fail between the two, leaving them out of step. Now the two writes are one commit.
  • Warehouse migrations get easier. Stored procedures from SQL Server, Synapse or Snowflake that wrap several writes in a transaction can move to Databricks with less rewriting.
  • Write-audit-publish in one step. Stage the data, record quality results and publish the good rows atomically.
  • Concurrent writers are fine. Row-level concurrency lets two transactions write the same table as long as they don't touch the same rows. Databricks claims a 4.7x speed-up for concurrent transactions at scale, without published benchmark details.

3. How it works

---
title: Optimistic transaction on the lakehouse
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant J as Job
    participant T as Transaction
    participant UC as Unity Catalog commit service
    J->>T: BEGIN ATOMIC
    T->>T: snapshot each table on first access
    T->>T: UPDATE orders, UPDATE inventory, INSERT audit_log
    T->>UC: commit all tables together
    UC-->>T: conflict check on changed rows
    UC-->>J: committed, or whole transaction fails

Transactions don't take locks. Each table is snapshotted the first time the transaction reads it, so reads are repeatable. Conflicts are checked only at commit. If another writer changed the same rows, the whole transaction fails and nothing is written. That is the same optimistic model Delta Lake already uses for single statements, now stretched across tables.

4. How to use it

Non-interactive, the usual choice for jobs (from the docs):

BEGIN ATOMIC
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
  INSERT INTO audit_log VALUES (1, 2, 100, current_timestamp());
END;

Interactive, for step-by-step work in a SQL warehouse session:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
-- check something, then
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK;

Statements allowed inside: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE INTO, COPY INTO, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, USE CATALOG/SCHEMA, DESCRIBE TABLE, SHOW COLUMNS, GET DIAGNOSTICS.

In practice, a checklist before you rely on it:

  1. Make sure the tables are Unity Catalog managed tables with catalog commits enabled. External and path-based tables don't qualify.
  2. Enable row-level concurrency on busy target tables, so parallel jobs don't fail each other.
  3. Move DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) out of the transaction block. It isn't allowed inside.
  4. Add a retry around the whole block for commit conflicts, just as you would around a single MERGE.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Limits: up to 100 tables read or written, up to 100 views and up to 100 intermediate commits per table in one transaction.
  • Timeouts: interactive transactions roll back after 10 minutes idle. Every transaction rolls back after 48 hours.
  • Not allowed inside: DDL, time travel and SHOW TABLES-style listing.
  • Optimistic means retries. Hot rows updated by many writers will see commit failures. Design for it.
  • Iceberg writes to managed Iceberg tables are still in private preview.
  • Lineage events persist even when a transaction rolls back.
  • Adopt now or wait? Use it now for new multi-table jobs and for migrating stored procedures. Leave single-table MERGE jobs alone. They were already atomic.

6. Where it fits

  • Delta Lake: the single-table ACID log this builds on.
  • Databricks platform: Unity Catalog, SQL warehouses and serverless compute.
  • Pipeline patterns and practices: write-audit-publish and idempotent loads.
  • Relational databases: the isolation levels and locking this is compared with.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What can go wrong in a two-table load without transactions, and how does BEGIN ATOMIC remove it?
  2. Why do lakehouse transactions use optimistic concurrency, not locks?
  3. When would you choose an interactive transaction over BEGIN ATOMIC?
  4. Two jobs update different rows of the same table at once. What setting decides whether both commit?
  5. Name three things you can't do inside a Databricks transaction.

Sources

  • Transactions — Databricks documentation
